bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- Physical climate risk to coastal and island assets — Flagged by the Company as a RISK with negative financial implications: 'Our high-value assets in coastal and island settings - Goa and the Maldives - face cyclones, storm surge and long-term sea-level rise, while our inland properties in Pune contend with urban flooding. A single severe event can damage property, disrupt operations, inflate insurance premiums and keep guests away in peak season.' Mitigation stated as climate-resilient specifications in new construction and major refurbishments, insurance updated against climate-adjusted loss models, climate-risk assumptions embedded in capital-expenditure decisions and physical-risk findings fed into the Board-level Risk Management framework. Structural because 515 of 2,199 keys are Maldivian island resorts and the newest India growth vector is coastal Goa.
- Water availability, tariffs and discharge compliance — Flagged as a RISK with negative implications: the Company operates 'from the water-stressed basins of Pune to island resorts in the Maldives that rely on energy-intensive desalination', and 'shrinking freshwater availability, rising municipal tariffs and tightening discharge norms make water both a material cost and a question of operational continuity'. Explicitly: 'any lapse against discharge norms would expose us to penalties.' Mitigation includes sewage treatment plants at all operational properties by FY 2026-27, reuse for landscaping/cooling/flushing, rainwater harvesting, greywater recycling and brine management at SWRO-equipped island resorts.
- Energy cost and grid dependence — Energy is stated to be 'among our largest operating costs' - hotels, offices and retail draw power continuously for HVAC, kitchens, laundry, lighting and shared areas - and 'a significant share still flows from the grid, leaving us exposed to tariff volatility and weighing materially on our Scope 2 footprint'. Framed by the Company as an opportunity, but the exposure to tariff volatility is a structural cost risk for an owner of energy-intensive luxury assets.
- Occupational health and safety, with incomplete certification coverage — Flagged as a RISK with negative implications: hotels carry 'a wide range of hazards - across kitchens, chemical handling, fire systems, electrical installations, pools and high-footfall public spaces - and a safety failure carries human, regulatory and reputational consequences'. Critically, the Company concedes that although it operates under ISO 45001:2018 and brand-operator safety frameworks, 'certification does not yet reach across our entire portfolio' and it is still 'extending ISO 45001 certification across our domestic portfolio'. Consequences named: compensation claims, regulatory penalties, operational downtime and reputational damage.
- Human-rights and labour risk in an outsourced, migrant-heavy value chain — Flagged as a RISK with negative implications: 'Our value chain draws on outsourced laundry, housekeeping, security and construction services, and on migrant workers at our Maldivian resorts - the very places where wage, working-hour and accommodation issues can arise', with rising expectations under BRSR Principle 5, the EU CSDDD and the OECD Guidelines. Violations 'would expose us to regulatory penalties, litigation, brand damage and lost investor confidence'. This compounds the workforce-structure disclosure below.
- Workforce structure and attrition - almost the entire workforce is non-permanent — A structural concentration visible in the BRSR headcount table rather than labelled as a risk: of 3,108 employees only 38 are permanent, 3,070 are 'other than permanent', and of 3 workers none are permanent - so service delivery in a luxury-service business rests almost entirely on non-permanent and outsourced labour. The Company separately acknowledges 'an industry marked by high attrition' and that women were 19.37% of the workforce in FY 2025-26 against a 30% target by FY 2029-30, with 0 of 3 KMP and 1 of 6 directors being women. Note the reported FY 2025-26 permanent-employee turnover of 2.78% covers only the 38 permanent staff; prior-year comparatives are printed 'NA' because FY 2025-26 is the first BRSR reporting year, so no trend can be read. [Headcount and diversity figures back-filled with provenance from the profile/registry sibling bundles - BRSR Section A.]
- Dependence on third-party brand operators and on guest sentiment — The Company is an asset owner whose promise 'rests on delivering service of consistent quality across six global brand standards: Marriott, Hilton, Anantara/Minor, Conrad, Oakwood and Atmosphere', and it states plainly that 'online reviews and social sentiment move our RevPAR directly'. Service standards are aligned with brand operators 'on an ongoing basis', i.e. day-to-day guest experience and therefore pricing power sit with counterparties the Company does not control. Note the operator list here (Anantara/Minor, Conrad, Oakwood, Atmosphere) differs from the Corporate Overview's '6 Hospitality Operators' list (Marriott International, Hilton Worldwide, Atmosphere Core, Minor Group, Ascott Hotels, Soho House & Co Inc.) - recorded as printed.
- Ecological licence risk at protected coastal and reef locations — Several properties 'sit in ecologically sensitive settings - coral-island resorts in the Maldives and coastal properties under Coastal Regulation Zone conditions - where the reef, the shoreline and the silence are the experience. Were these to degrade, we would risk both our construction licences and the very destination magic on which our luxury positioning rests.' Compliance depends on Maldives EPA approvals and CRZ conditions, so both existing operations and the development pipeline carry permit risk.
- Food-safety exposure at luxury properties — Flagged as material: 'Our food and beverage operations contribute a significant share of our revenue, and a single food-safety incident at a luxury property can do bra[nd damage]' - the disclosure is truncated mid-sentence in the routed text, so the mitigation column for this topic is unavailable. Relevant given the stated 70+ F&B offerings across the portfolio.
- Geographic and asset concentration — Not labelled a risk by the Company but disclosed structurally: operations span only 3 Indian states and 1 international country (BRSR Section A), the Pune cluster carries six hotels plus all four commercial annuity assets, and the 'social licence to operate matters most around our flagship Pune cluster and the island communities that neighbour our Maldivian resorts'. Two subsidiaries (Nagenahira Resorts, KBJ Hotel & Restaurants) are yet to commence operations, so the Sri Lanka leg is committed capital not yet earning. [Concentration facts back-filled with provenance from the profile/registry sibling bundles.]
- Macro, geopolitical and travel-cost sensitivity of discretionary demand — The Board's Report and MD&A name geopolitical and economic uncertainty, prolonged conflicts, inflation and financial volatility, high travel costs and a traveller shift toward 'value for money' as factors that may affect travel patterns in 2026; management records that 'global travel demand witnessed periods of uncertainty during the year, influenced by evolving geopolitical developments, including tensions in parts of the Middle East'. India's international tourist arrivals themselves moderated 2.4% to 20.09 Mn in 2025. The cautionary statement adds economic developments, pricing and demand-supply conditions, changes in government regulations, tax laws, litigation and industrial relations as factors that could influence operations. [Macro items back-filled with provenance from the strategy_outlook sibling bundle.]

business.title: Segment / subsidiary detail

business.body:
- Headline platform claim: "India's Largest Luxury Focused Hospitality Platform" with 14 hotels, 3 countries, 2,199 keys and 80% luxury focus.
- Six-part value proposition: strong cashflow generation (~₹8,000 Mn in FY26) to fund pipeline and acquisitions; active asset management with consistent EBITDA growth (+28% in FY26); lowest leverage amongst asset owners at Net Debt/EBITDA of 1.2x with <7% blended cost of financing; an annuity backbone against hospitality cyclicity; a strong operator network of 6 global operators and 14 brands; and promoters Panchshil and Blackstone combining local construction expertise with international best practices.
- Annuity backbone: total annuity assets of 3.40 Msf at 98% committed occupancy, described as "Integrated Commercial & Retail Assets Feed the Hotel Business and Generate Steady Annuity Income" and as assets with "Strong Entry Barriers, Geographically Diversified".
- Maldives moat framing: high entry barriers from the "one island, one resort" concept and limited land availability; the deck's island-peer chart places Maldives at ADR $1,200-1,300 with ~100 flights, and cites US$5.4bn of 2025 tourism revenue (+16% YoY, MMA) and World's Leading Destination recognition for 6 years running.
- Pune demand thesis: 500+ GCCs in Pune (FY26, 14% of India's total) growing at ~9% CAGR FY19-25 toward 700-750 GCCs by 2030, with Pune's top tier described as "structurally supply-protected" because there is "No luxury hotel pipeline and only modest upper-upscale additions".
business.title: Positioning (investor deck)

business.body:
- [Acquisition] Ritz-Carlton Reserve, Sahyadri Hills - acquisition completed in Jul'26 with OC received, extending the platform into luxury wellness hospitality 2-3 hours from Mumbai and Pune and 45 minutes from Alibaug.
- [External shock] West Asia war drove Maldives diesel to $1.5-1.7/L at peak, >2x pre-war levels (+100% from July'25 to April-May'26, then -26% by July'26), causing +₹200 Mn of increased fuel and ancillary costs with >50% of FY26 fuel cost incurred in one quarter; Maldives arrivals for April-June'26 were 422K (-13% YoY).
- [Ownership/consolidation] All presentation details consider a 100% stake in Ritz-Carlton Pune and Raaya by Atmosphere; the Company owns 50%+ economic interest in Panchshil Corporate Park Pvt Ltd (PCPPL) and Kudakurathu Island Resorts Private Limited (KIRPL); Ventive owns 12.25% economic interest in the entity owning Soho House Mumbai, which is therefore not consolidated and is treated as a joint venture.
- [Tax] The deck attributes the Q1FY27 PAT step-up to a "transition to new tax regime" rather than operations.
- [Market data] Pune Grade-A office stock is shown at 95 Msf in Q1 2026 rising to ~140 Msf by 2030E (+47%, CBRE, broader market incl. PCMC), with the GCC share of Grade-A leasing at 55% in CY2025 and 69% in Q1 2026; the deck's incremental room-night estimate of 700-1,000 base case and 200-300 luxury/upper-upscale is explicitly flagged as "a sensitivity range - not a fixed industry conversion rule".
business.title: Notable from the deck

business.body: The Company owns, develops and asset-manages hotels, resorts and serviced residences that are operated under third-party global hotel flags, and separately owns and leases office and retail space that sits alongside those hotels in mixed-use destinations. The AR states it 'participates across the full asset lifecycle, from development and strategic positioning to operations and long-term performance management' and that its 'integrated approach allows us to create dynamic mixed-use destinations where hospitality, commercial, and retail spaces strengthen one another, driving embedded demand and enhancing asset value'. Customers span B2B (hotel brand partners under whose flags it operates, corporates contracting bulk crew accommodation, corporate tenants of leased commercial space) and B2C (in-house guests at hotels and serviced apartments, F&B patrons, retail tenants and walk-in customers at mixed-use developments). BRSR Section A names two activities accounting for 90% of turnover: 'Accommodation and Food Services' (NIC 551) at 79% of turnover and 'Real Estate — real estate activities with own or leased property' (NIC 701) at 19.04%.

outlook.body:
- Theme for FY 2026 is 'Curated Growth, Driven by People' - growth is to be 'intentional, well-judged, and supported by the right mix of people, partnerships, and capabilities', and this philosophy governs how opportunities are evaluated and the platform scaled. [Back-filled with provenance from the profile sibling bundle - the Management Message itself was routed there, not to this bundle.]
- Disciplined expansion, operational consistency and long-term value creation as the three stated pillars, building on 'over two decades of experience and the strategic direction established in our first year as a listed company'. [profile sibling bundle - Management Message.]
- Portfolio expansion by acquisition of operating assets rather than greenfield alone: Hilton Goa Resort, Sol de Goa, Soho House Mumbai and Narmada Estates were added, each intended to strengthen 'positioning across key leisure and urban markets, while contributing to the development of a more balanced portfolio anchored by a strong annuity backbone'. [profile sibling bundle - Management Message; transaction mechanics in the capex_expansion sibling.]
- Drive operating performance across existing assets 'through disciplined cost management, targeted demand generation, and enhanced guest experiences', so growth is sustained without diluting portfolio quality. [profile sibling bundle.]
- Segment diversification away from a pure India-business-hotel base: entry into leisure (Hilton Goa Resort, Sol de Goa), into the membership-based lifestyle segment (Soho House Mumbai, with exclusive Soho House India expansion rights), and international leisure (Maldives, with Sri Lanka underway). [profile sibling bundle - 'scaling across geographies'; Soho House exclusivity from the capex_expansion sibling.]
- Ownership-led operating model retained - own, develop and asset-manage while global operators flag the assets, so the Company 'participates across the full asset lifecycle' with six brand partners rather than building an in-house brand. [profile sibling bundle.]
- Corporate-structure simplification: a scheme of amalgamation of EON-Hinjewadi Infrastructure, Restocraft Hospitality and Wellcraft Infraprojects into the listed entity was filed with the NCLT on 12th September 2025.
- Retain earnings for growth rather than distribute - no dividend recommended for FY26, no transfer to General Reserves, surplus retained in the Profit and Loss Account, with a Dividend Distribution Policy formulated under Regulation 43A.
- Responsible growth: continued commitment to 'strong governance', with 'environmental efficiency, resource management, and community engagement' embedded in operations 'ensuring that our growth is both sustainable and future-ready'. [profile sibling bundle; the quantified ESG targets sit in the risks_esg sibling.]
- Pune-anchored compounding: the Company frames its future hospitality pipeline in Pune as positioned to support the city's next growth phase 'by adding capacity, strengthening our presence across high-potential locations, and deepening the city's premium hospitality infrastructure'. [capex_expansion sibling bundle - 'Building Pune's Hospitality Future'.]
- Stated philosophy is full retention for growth. The Board 'do[es] not recommend any dividend for the year ended 31st March 2026' expressly 'to retain the profits for future growth of the Company', while confirming that a Dividend Distribution Policy has been formulated as required by Regulation 43A of the SEBI Listing Regulations and is published on the Company's website. No amount is proposed to be transferred to General Reserves - the surplus is retained in the Profit and Loss Account. During the year there was no bonus issue, no buy-back, and no issue of shares with differential voting rights, sweat equity or employee stock options; the authorised share capital was unchanged; and no deposits within the meaning of Sections 73-74 were accepted or outstanding. Growth funding is therefore internal accrual plus debt at the asset level, with the group extending a corporate guarantee for subsidiary borrowing (Kudakurathu Island Resort, guarantee running to 31st March 2033). On the cost of that capital, the Financial Highlights spread claims the 'Lowest cost of debt among pure-play asset owners, ~7.3% p.a. and AA Stable rating from CRISIL' [back-filled with provenance from the profile sibling bundle]. Capital deployment in the year went to acquisitions of operating assets (Hilton Goa Resort via a 76% stake in Soham Leisure Ventures; Soho House Mumbai and the exclusive Soho House India expansion rights via Finest-VN Business Park), continued after the year end (Sol de Goa; 50.02% of Narmada Estates), and is accompanied by a structural simplification - the NCLT scheme filed 12th September 2025 to amalgamate three subsidiaries into the listed entity.
- Renewable electricity: 'we ... hold ourselves to a 50% renewable electricity share by FY 2029-30', pursued through open-access solar and wind contracts at eligible properties plus rooftop solar, Building Management Systems for HVAC and lighting loads, and portfolio-wide LED retrofits.
- Water intensity: 'holding ourselves to a 15% reduction in water intensity by FY 2029-30'.
- Sewage treatment: 'We are installing on-site Sewage Treatment Plants at all operational properties by FY 2026-27' with treated water reused for landscaping, cooling towers and flushing; rainwater harvesting and greywater recycling being expanded; brine discharge managed at SWRO-equipped island resorts.
- Net zero: 'We are committing to net-zero operations by FY 2049-50, with interim milestones on renewable electricity, refrigerant transition and energy efficiency.'
- Decarbonisation roadmap: 'We will complete a Scope 3 screening and a portfolio-wide decarbonisation roadmap in FY 2026-27', and climate disclosures are being aligned progressively with IFRS S2. The Company states it has 'established an externally assured emissions baseline' while conceding 'our Scope 3 inventory and a validated transition plan are still taking shape'.
- Green buildings and safety certification: pursuing LEED and IGBC green-building certifications; extending ISO 45001 certification across the domestic portfolio, with periodic fire and food-safety audits network-wide, on-site clinics and resident physicians at Maldivian resorts.
- Waste and circularity: segregation at source across all properties, food waste processed through on-site biogas units, hazardous and e-waste routed through authorised handlers with full manifest tracking, single-use plastics being phased out of guest-facing areas, and housekeeping and laundry chemicals transitioning to green-certified alternatives.
- Biodiversity: compliance with Maldives EPA approvals and CRZ conditions at all relevant properties, coral gardening and reef-monitoring programmes at island resorts, elimination of single-use plastic bottles through on-site glass-bottled water, and periodic 3D reef mapping and biodiversity surveys.
- Diversity: women were 19.37% of the workforce in FY 2025-26 against a stated 'target of 30% by FY 2029-30'; the Company also holds itself to 'a 100% maternity return-to-work and retention rate', runs a multi-brand management-trainee programme with internal talent mobility, and ensures accessibility compliance under the RPwD Act, 2016.
- Human rights: a Human Rights Due Diligence policy with confidentiality and anti-retaliation safeguards, a Supplier Code of Conduct covering labour standards, wages and working hours, third-party audits of high-risk suppliers, grievance channels extended to contract and migrant workers, and POSH Internal Committees at all applicable properties.
- Guest-experience governance: brand-specific SOP audits with Net Promoter Score and Guest Satisfaction Surveys tracked monthly at property and corporate level, and real-time monitoring of OTA and social-media sentiment.
- Materiality process: 'The Company conducted a materiality assessment during FY 2025-26, benchmarked against leading Indian hospitality peers, based on stakeholder input and business impact. Out of the identified universe of issues, fourteen material topics covering environmental, social and governance dimensions have been prioritised', with the assessment refreshed annually with stakeholder input. FY 2025-26 is the Company's first BRSR reporting year.
- Assurance: BRSR prepared on a consolidated basis with 'Reasonable Assurance' from IQRS (India) Private Limited. [Back-filled with provenance from the profile/registry sibling bundles - BRSR Section A items 13-15.]
- Green capex: '9.71% of the Company's total capital expenditure for FY 2025-26 was directed towards technologies that improve environmental and social impacts, principally renewable energy (rooftop solar PV), energy-efficient HVAC and heat-pump systems, low-GWP refrigeration, smart building controls and metering, wastewater treatment and water-recycling infrastructure, and fire and life-safety systems', against 0 in FY 2024-25. R&D spend on such technologies is a stated nil - 'The Company hasn't carried a formal research and development function or associated expenditure.' [Back-filled with provenance from the capex_expansion sibling bundle - BRSR Principle 2.]
- Ethics: an Anti-Corruption and Anti-Bribery Policy applying to all directors, officers, employees, contractors and business partners, reinforced by a whistleblower mechanism with anti-retaliation protection and reviewed periodically by the Board; zero disciplinary actions for bribery or corruption against directors, KMPs, employees or workers in the current and previous year; nil conflict-of-interest complaints; a Code of Conduct for Board and Senior Management under which interested directors recuse themselves and abstain from voting. [Back-filled with provenance from the capex_expansion sibling bundle - BRSR Principle 1.]
- Sustainable sourcing: 'The Company's Supplier Code of Conduct encourages local sourcing, environmentally responsible packaging, and compliance with labour and safety standards. Key suppliers are assessed against these criteria' (sentence truncated in the routed text). [capex_expansion sibling bundle - BRSR Principle 2.]
- STATED ABSENCE, recorded as a finding: value-chain awareness programmes on the NGRBC Principles were NIL in FY 2025-26 - 'the Company did not conduct structured awareness programmes for its value chain partners', relying instead on routine commercial interactions, and 'intends to progressively introduce structured awareness and capability-building initiatives ... in the forthcoming reporting periods'. [capex_expansion sibling bundle.]
- STATED ABSENCE, recorded as a finding: zero grievances were received in FY 2025-26 and FY 2024-25 across every stakeholder category in the BRSR complaints table - communities, investors other than shareholders, shareholders, employees and workers, customers and value-chain partners - all printed as '0 / No complaints'; and nil sexual-harassment complaints were received, disposed of or pending beyond ninety days. A universal zero across a 3,100-person, multi-country workforce is recorded as printed and flagged as implausibly clean rather than treated as evidence of no issues.

outlook.body: Ventive's expansion is asset acquisition and key addition, not plant capex. WITHIN FY 2025-26 the Board's Report records two completed acquisitions: (i) a 76% stake in Soham Leisure Ventures Private Limited, 'the owning entity of Hilton Goa Resort', on 15th October 2025, making it a subsidiary; and (ii) through material step-down subsidiary Panchshil Corporate Park Private Limited, a 100% stake in Finest-VN Business Park Private Limited on 17 February 2026 - Finest-VN 'through its subsidiaries, holds the exclusive rights for the expansion of Soho House in India and operates Soho House Mumbai (Juhu)'. AFTER the financial year, two further acquisitions closed: Soham acquired 100% of Sun Leisure India Private Limited, owner of the hotel Sol de Goa, and Panchshil Corporate Park acquired 50.02% of Narmada Estates Private Limited. The consolidated accounts add the mechanics of both (back-filled with provenance from the governance_entities sibling bundle, Note 51): the Narmada SPA is dated 15th April 2026 for a 50.02% equity stake 'for a total consideration of J 886.80 million', and 'Narmada owns a land parcel in the vicinity of the existing hotel of PCPPL, "The Ritz-Carlton, Pune'; the Sun Leisure SPA is dated 7th April 2026 for 100% 'for a total consideration of J 5.00 million'. The milestone spread frames the trajectory: '~2x Growth in keys - From 1,164 keys in 2021 to 2,199 keys in 2026 ... with a clear roadmap to achieve ~4,000 keys by 2031', with 2025 marked by the 'Signing of new hotels comprising 1,382 keys with Marriott International in India and Sri Lanka'. THE DECLARED PIPELINE (from the Geographical Presence spread, back-filled with provenance from the profile sibling bundle) is: Moxy Pune Wakad 264 keys; Moxy Pune Kharadi 200 keys; AC by Marriott, Bengaluru - 166 keys rebranding of the existing Aloft Bengaluru Whitefield plus 33 additional keys; JW Marriott Navi Mumbai 450 keys; Moxy Navi Mumbai 200 keys; Soho House New Delhi (Mehrauli) 24 keys; Varanasi Marriott Hotel 161 keys; the commercial annuity asset Narmada Estates, Pune 0.63 msf; and in Sri Lanka, Pottuvil, a Ritz-Carlton Reserve, with 73 villas plus 80 branded residences. Within the existing portfolio, Hilton Goa Resort (104 keys) is printed as 'expanding key count by ~50+ keys and branded luxury villas'. The AR disclaims that 'the proposed key counts are indicative in nature and are subject to change as the projects advance' and that the brand names 'represent hotel brands expected to be added to the Company's portfolio and are for indicative purposes only' - no commissioning or completion date is attached to ANY of these projects anywhere in the routed text. Two owned entities are still pre-operational: 'NAGENAHIRA RESORTS (PVT) LTD and KBJ HOTEL & RESTAURANTS PRIVATE LIMITED is yet to commence operations'. Structural expansion is also being pursued through corporate action: a scheme of amalgamation of EON-Hinjewadi Infrastructure, Restocraft Hospitality and Wellcraft Infraprojects into Ventive Hospitality Limited was filed with the NCLT on 12th September 2025. On the geography of future build-out, the 'Building Pune's Hospitality Future' chapter states that 'our future hospitality pipeline in the city is positioned to support the next phase of this expansion' by 'adding capacity, strengthening our presence across high-potential locations, and deepening the city's premium hospitality infrastructure', citing Pune's 500+ GCCs expected to grow to 660-680 by 2030 and office space rising from 100 million sq. ft. to 145 million sq. ft. by 2030 (KPMG). The only capex-composition figure disclosed in narrative form is from BRSR Principle 2: '9.71% of the Company's total capital expenditure for FY 2025-26 was directed towards technologies that improve environmental and social impacts, principally renewable energy (rooftop solar PV), energy-efficient HVAC and heat-pump systems, low-GWP refrigeration, smart building controls and metering, wastewater treatment and water-recycling infrastructure, and fire and life-safety systems' (prior year: 0). R&D capex is a stated nil - 'The Company hasn't carried a formal research and development function or associated expenditure.' outlook.body:
- India macro: GDP grew 7.6% in FY 2026 against 7.1% in FY 2025 (MoSPI new series, base 2022-23), supported by strong domestic demand, policy reforms and recovering private and public investment; 'sectors such as trade, hotels, transport, and communication witnessed a strong recovery'. The RBI cut the repo rate in phases as inflation eased.
- Rising per-capita income is cited as a demand driver - 'per capita income has been rising and is expected to increase from $ 2,675 in 2025 to $ 3,075 in 2027' - alongside urbanisation, a young workforce and an expanding middle class.
- Global tourism outlook for 2026 remains positive with tourism 'expected to grow by 3-4% year-over-year', helped by the FIFA World Cup 2026 and the Milano Cortina 2026 Winter Olympics; offsetting factors named are geopolitical tensions, high travel costs, economic uncertainty and a traveller shift toward value for money. International tourist arrivals reached ~1.52 Bn in 2025, +4% over 2024 and above pre-pandemic levels; Asia-Pacific ITAs ~331 Mn, +6%.
- Indian hospitality is structurally undersupplied - 'an undersupplied market in which demand outpaced available room inventory' - with 2025 occupancy 64% (+1.1 pts), ADR H 8,624 (+8.6%) and RevPAR H 5,522 (+10.8%). Branded inventory ~133,000 rooms; total inventory ~216,000 rooms (+7.7% YoY); pipeline expanded by 39,000 rooms to 144,000, implying ~360,000 rooms by 2030 if all planned projects complete.
- GCC-led corporate demand is the named new demand pool: GCCs 'attract large volumes of business travel, long-stay corporate guests, training visits, client meetings, and relocation-related stays' in Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Pune and Delhi-NCR, lifting weekday occupancy and stabilising year-round demand across mid-scale to luxury.
- Pune - the Company's flagship market - is described as supply-constrained at the top end: room supply grew only 757 rooms since 2019 against 654 rooms of demand growth, Lux-Upper Upscale ADR crossed H 10,000 in 2025, city-wide occupancy reached 70.5% (strongest among India's non-metro business markets), and 'the forward supply pipeline contains no new luxury hotels and only modest Upper Upscale rooms'. Pune city 2025 metrics: ~70.5% occupancy, ADR ~H 7,000, RevPAR ~H 5,000. Future connectivity from the Navi Mumbai International Airport and better road infrastructure is expected to help.
- Maldives market sizing: valued at ~$2.87 Bn in 2025, projected $3.13 Bn in 2026 and $4.78 Bn by 2031 at 8.87% CAGR (Mordor Intelligence). Luxury held the largest share at 51.24% in 2025 and is expected to grow at 11.37% CAGR to 2031; independent hotels held 57.87% share while chain hotels are expected to grow at 9.29% CAGR. Supportive: Velana International Airport upgrades, new direct long-haul routes, government incentives and faster approvals. Structural negatives named: high import dependency and climate vulnerability.
- Demand-mix drivers named for India: business travel, MICE, weddings, hybrid travel and workcations lengthening average stays and improving asset utilisation, and premiumisation from rising disposable incomes and preference for premium experiences, luxury stays and wellness tourism.
- Segment-mix backdrop: Luxury and Upper Upscale account for more than 20% of room inventory in most markets (lower in Mumbai), with Goa ~45% and Jaipur ~55%.
- Forward supply concentration to watch, 2026-2030: Bengaluru is expected to lead with ~11,400 new rooms and Delhi NCR ~9,300 - both markets where the Company has existing or upcoming assets.
- India international tourist arrivals moderated - 20.09 Mn in 2025 (provisional) versus 20.57 Mn in 2024, a 2.4% decline from a high base - a stated negative within an otherwise positive demand narrative.
- Company-level positioning statement in the Board's Report: 'With a diversified portfolio across India and the Maldives and exposure to both high-growth domestic demand and premium international leisure destinations, Ventive Hospitality is well-positioned to benefit from sustained industry tailwinds and the continued shift towards luxury, experience-led travel.'
- Management's own framing of the international backdrop: 'global travel demand witnessed periods of uncertainty during the year, influenced by evolving geopolitical developments, including tensions in parts of the Middle East. However, demand across our international portfolio remained resilient' - with 'supply-side constraints in premium segments' expected to support long-term value creation. [profile sibling bundle - Management Message.]
- Hospitality has no order book; the analogue disclosed is the development pipeline. Upcoming projects printed in the 'Geographical Presence' spread: Moxy Pune Wakad (264 keys), Moxy Pune Kharadi (200 keys), AC by Marriott Bengaluru (166 keys rebranding + 33 additional keys), JW Marriott Navi Mumbai (450 keys), Moxy Navi Mumbai (200 keys), Soho House New Delhi, Mehrauli (24 keys), Varanasi Marriott Hotel (161 keys), the commercial annuity asset Narmada Estates, Pune (0.63 msf), and Pottuvil, a Ritz-Carlton Reserve, Sri Lanka (73 villas + 80 branded residences). The AR disclaims that 'the proposed key counts are indicative in nature and are subject to change as the projects advance' and that the brand names 'represent hotel brands expected to be added ... and are for indicative purposes only'. [Back-filled with provenance from the profile sibling bundle.]
- Signed pipeline with a named counterparty: 'Signing of new hotels comprising 1,382 keys with Marriott International in India and Sri Lanka' (2025 milestone). [Back-filled with provenance from the capex_expansion sibling bundle - milestones spread.]
- Stated roadmap: '~2x Growth in keys - From 1,164 keys in 2021 to 2,199 keys in 2026 ... with a clear roadmap to achieve ~4,000 keys by 2031.' [capex_expansion sibling bundle.]
- Two owned entities are pre-operational and therefore represent committed but unearning capacity: 'NAGENAHIRA RESORTS (PVT) LTD and KBJ HOTEL & RESTAURANTS PRIVATE LIMITED is yet to commence operations'. [profile/registry sibling bundles - BRSR Section A.]

risks.note: Flagged as a RISK with negative implications: the Company operates 'from the water-stressed basins of Pune to island resorts in the Maldives that rely on energy-intensive desalination', and 'shrinking freshwater availability, rising municipal tariffs and tightening discharge norms make water both a material cost and a question of operational continuity'. Explicitly: 'any lapse against discharge norms would expose us to penalties.' Mitigation includes sewage treatment plants at all operational properties by FY 2026-27, reuse for landscaping/cooling/flushing, rainwater harvesting, greywater recycling and brine management at SWRO-equipped island resorts.

risks.note: Energy is stated to be 'among our largest operating costs' - hotels, offices and retail draw power continuously for HVAC, kitchens, laundry, lighting and shared areas - and 'a significant share still flows from the grid, leaving us exposed to tariff volatility and weighing materially on our Scope 2 footprint'. Framed by the Company as an opportunity, but the exposure to tariff volatility is a structural cost risk for an owner of energy-intensive luxury assets.

Flagged as a RISK with negative implications: hotels carry 'a wide range of hazards - across kitchens, chemical handling, fire systems, electrical installations, pools and high-footfall public spaces - and a safety failure carries human, regulatory and reputational consequences'. Consequences named: compensation claims, regulatory penalties, operational downtime and reputational damage.
